doc.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

chapter: Monk, the Army and learning the job
title: What Monk taught him about the studio and about criticism
summary: He learned attitudes, patience with demanding artists and distrust of jazz criticism, with Monk's remark to Hawkins.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: All right. The early things with Monk certainly must have opened your ears up and it seems like some of the stuff that he taught you might not have been apparent right at that
time? Was there kind of like a delay in certain incidents where you understood afterwards what he was trying to show you?

Well no, when I talk about learning from Monk, to me the most important learning from Monk that I did was a matter of learning attitudes. Learning how to conduct myself in the studio in relation to the important, demanding, impatient artist, which is what all good artists should be. And it wasn’t so much — I did discover for example that — eventually I discovered that the main cause of Monk’s impatience, and his impatience with his fellow musicians, was that as far as he was concerned there wasn’t anything that difficult about his music. He grasped it. How come you couldn’t? One of my favorite lines which happens to have survived on a scrap of tape from a session that Coleman Hawkins and John Coltrane were involved in is Hawkins had been having trouble with the turnaround on one particular number and Monk can be heard saying to him, “whatsa matter? You’re supposed to be the great Coleman Hawkins. How come you can’t play that?” He didn’t say you’re the great Coleman Hawkins how come you can’t — you’re supposed to be the great Coleman Hawkins. I’ve always treasured that remark. But fundamentally it’s that I, again, understanding what I consider to be the root causes of his impatience which were that he didn’t know what the hell was it that was giving you this trouble. I’m not having any trouble with this. And that he was an excellent teacher as far as logistics is concerned. I learned how to conduct myself in the studio, I learned when to push, when not to push, and how much of that has got to be instinctive and is a matter of reading what the artist has in mind, and I also learned to be very wary of arbitrary musical judgements. I think this is perhaps one of the things that has led to my lifelong distaste for and distrust of jazz criticism. Because it has always been full of people who feel that it’s necessary for them to strike a pose, to take a position, to give us THE judgment from heaven as to whether this is good or that is bad or whatnot. And you know that’s not necessary. And it’s never been necessary. Music is something that gets evaluated very personally. I mean yeah, proficient playing and non-proficient playing is generally, you can make distinctions there, except a hell of a lot of people spent a lot of time in the early days saying that Monk couldn’t play the piano and they were wrong. But in general I just feel that — now value judgements are very important. I have lots of value judgements and have always made such judgements, and I have only under very rare and unusual circumstances allowed myself to get involved professionally with a musician that I didn’t have strong positive feelings for, but that didn’t necessarily have to involve compatibility between two — I can approve of two musicians who wouldn’t necessarily approve of each other, approaching them from — and I’ve never felt it necessary for there to be an arbitrary set of standards and I’m very wary of judging performances.
